ready1_open_rewrite.raw_question_text:
Jakob writes one of the natural numbers 1 to 9 into each cell of the $3 \times 3$-table. Then he works out the sum of the numbers in each row and in each column. Five of his results are 12, 13, 15, 16 and 17. What is the sixth sum?

ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Graph description: In the figure is an empty 3×3 grid table, with 3 rows and 3 columns. Therefore Jakob will get 3 row sums and 3 column sums, a total of 6 sums. Reasoning: The problem states that the nine numbers from 1 to 9 are respectively filled into the nine cells, so the total sum of the numbers in all cells is 1+2+3+4+5+6+7+8+9=45. The sum of the three row sums equals the total sum of all cells, 45; the sum of the three column sums also equals the total sum of all cells, 45. Therefore the total sum of the 6 row/column sums is 45+45=90. It is known that five of the sums are 12, 13, 15, 16, 17, and their sum is 12+13+15+16+17=73. So the sixth sum is 90-73=17.

method.method_draft: Use a global double-counting invariant. From the image, note that the table has 3 rows and 3 columns, giving exactly 6 row/column sums. From the text, take the entries to be the numbers 1 through 9 placed in the nine cells, so the total of all cell entries is 1+2+...+9=45. The sum of the three row sums is 45, and the sum of the three column sums is also 45, so the total of all six reported sums is 90. The five given sums add to 12+13+15+16+17=73, so the missing sixth sum is 90-73=17.

method.method_draft: Use the fact that the six sums must split into two triples: the three row sums and the three column sums. From the image, identify that there are exactly three rows and three columns. From the text, the total of all entries is 1+2+...+9=45, so the three row sums must form a triple totaling 45, and the three column sums must also form a triple totaling 45. Since five of the six sums are known, one of the row/column triples is entirely among the known five. Among 12, 13, 15, 16, 17, the possible triples summing to 45 are 12+16+17 and 13+15+17. If the complete known triple is 12,16,17, then the other triple contains 13,15 and the unknown, so the unknown is 45-13-15=17. If the complete known triple is 13,15,17, then the other triple contains 12,16 and the unknown, so the unknown is 45-12-16=17. In either case, the sixth sum is 17.
